title: Determinants of recovery from a 161-km ultramarathon
authors: Hoffman MD, Badowski N, Chin J, Stuempfle KJ, Parise CA
population: 72 finishers of a 161-km ultramarathon with 400 m max-speed runs before the race and on days 3 and 5, a post-race blood sample, and daily soreness and fatigue ratings pre-race and for 7 days
findings: Soreness (10-point scale) and overall muscular fatigue (100-point scale) had statistically returned to pre-race levels by 5 days post-race.
400 m run times at day 3 and day 5 remained 26% (P = 0.001) and 12% (P = 0.01) slower than pre-race.

Post-race creatine kinase best modelled soreness, fatigue and per cent change in 400 m time: runners with the highest CKs had 1.5 points higher soreness (P < 0.001) and 11.2 points higher fatigue (P = 0.006) than runners with the lowest.
A significant time x CK interaction (P < 0.001) indicates higher CK was linked with a slower rate of return to pre-race 400 m time.
limitations: Online 2016, issue year 2017; 400 m speed test is a narrow performance proxy and was done only to day 5 (ratings to day 7); post-race CK is not available to a plan engine; self-report at a single event.
implications: After a 100-mile race, subjective soreness and fatigue can look normal by day 5 while maximal 400 m speed is still 12% down: a normal-looking check-in must not shorten the hold or advance the ramp. Check-ins can gate only in the cautious direction (delay or repeat a step).
Supports no speed or maximal-effort work for at least the first 5 to 7 days and a speed-free return beyond that, since speed was the slowest function to recover in this study (no data past day 5).
Runners with the most muscle damage recover slowest, so a plan could offer a longer default for hard-raced or hilly efforts, though the engine has no CK input.

verification.notes: Crossref (J Sports Sci, online 2016-05-11, authors match) and abstract re-read (PMID 27167683). All numbers match. Limitation text corrected: the abstract has ratings for 7 days and 400 m runs to day 5.
